summary: A commentary on the recommendation that IANA begin giving out unallocated parts of the old Class A address space as classless blocks. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The biggest blocks of addresses were being cut into smaller pieces. This note discusses what that means.

questions: what happened to unallocated class a blocks
why does class a deployment require classless routing
what are the guidelines for allocating class a addresses
what routing problems occur when mixing class-full and classless domains
subtitle: Implications of allocating the unallocated Class A address space classlessly.

tldr.problem: The Internet Address Lifetime Expectancy Working Group proposed allocating the remaining 25% of the Class A address space (the largest remaining unallocated pool) as classless prefixes instead of waiting for Class C exhaustion to force changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the routing implications for network service providers and non-transit networks, showing that deployment of Class A prefixes requires widespread adoption of classless (CIDR) interior routing protocols rather than traditional class-full routing.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends guidelines for which networks should receive Class A allocations, emphasizing that a transition to uniform classless routing is necessary and desirable for continued efficient Internet operation. It is now historic.

today: RFC 2036 is historic. The Internet did transition to classless routing; CIDR and classless interior routing protocols became the norm. Class A space was allocated and deployed during this transition. This document's analysis was prescient in identifying the routing changes required, and those changes did occur as predicted.

sections.title: Background on Address Space and the Proposal
sections.content:
Internet addresses are organized into classes: Class A (first octet 1–126, providing over 16 million addresses each), Class B (first octet 128–191, providing 65,000 addresses each), and Class C (first octet 192–223, providing 256 addresses each). By 1996, Class C addresses were being exhausted, with approximately 25% of the Class A space (roughly half the Class A range) still unallocated.

Traditionally, network allocations followed class-full boundaries: a Class A network, a Class B network, or multiple Class C networks. However, Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) enabled classless address blocks—arbitrary-length prefix allocations that cross class boundaries. The RFC examines the implications of the proposed recommendation that IANA allocate unallocated Class A space as classless prefixes to registries for deployment in the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three sizes of address blocks (Class A, B, and C), and the biggest ones (Class A) have lots unused. Instead of giving out those big blocks the old way, the idea was to cut them into any size and use the new classless system. The question is what problems that creates.

sections.title: Current Practice and Class-Full Routing
sections.content:
Until the 1996 timeframe, allocation practice conservatively used addresses compatible with Class C superblocks while maintaining Class A and Class B allocations aligned with class-based structures. Within this environment, non-transit networks could continue using class-full interior routing protocols with fixed subnet structures. Interior routing protocols such as RIP and OSPF could use class-full routing knowledge, relying on default routes or explicit sink routes to handle unreachable subnets.

For network service providers (transit domains), interior routing could use either aggregated or explicit class-full routing, with aggregated routes advertised at peering boundaries. The key assumption was that address allocations would remain aligned with class boundaries, so a single default route plus class-full routing information could successfully direct traffic. This assumption breaks down when Class A prefixes (which do not align with class boundaries) are deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system was simple: you could assume that everything starting with a certain number was one complete block, and if you did not know about part of it, you could use the default path. That worked when blocks aligned with the big/medium/small class sizes.

sections.title: Requirements for Class A Deployment
sections.content:
Deployment of classless Class A prefixes requires network service providers to deploy Class-less Interior Routing Protocols (CIRP) such as OSPF and IS-IS, even if they operate with a default route imported from peer providers. When a Class A prefix is allocated and advertised alongside a default route, class-full routers cannot distinguish whether the Class A is the complete network or just a component, leading to incorrect routing decisions.

For non-transit networks (which do not carry transit traffic), the implications differ by connectivity model. Disconnected networks face no additional constraints. Networks with a single default connection to a class-less provider can deploy Class A space using class-full interior routing if they explicitly route a subnet default route to the provider and configure sink routes for non-deployed parts. Networks multiply homed to multiple providers or connected to other peer networks must use class-less interior routing themselves. The RFC identifies scenarios where mixed routing (some domains class-full, some classless) creates routing holes, where traffic destined for certain parts of a Class A network cannot reach its destination because of incompatible routing assumptions at different domains.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get a Class A address block, your routers must use the new classless system, or traffic will get lost. If you connect to other networks, they have to use the new system too, or they will send your traffic to the wrong place. It creates a chain reaction—once one network deploys Class A space, nearby networks have to update too.

sections.title: Guidelines and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC proposes guidelines that Class A addresses should only be assigned to networks that: (1) have no external connection and can use either class-full or classless routing, (2) are part of a private internet where no other part of the Class A is assigned and all nodes use class-full routing, (3) have a single external connection to a classless routing provider and use class-full interior routing with explicit subnet default routing, or (4) use classless interior routing and connect only to other classless domains.

Recommended activities to enable Class A deployment include vendors implementing explicit router configuration for class-less versus class-full operation modes with correct default route behavior, development of host configuration tools supporting local network prefix assignment in addition to class-based configuration, and ISP support for full classless configurations in interior routing and interdomain peering with proxy aggregation. The core recommendation is that network domains should use classless interior routing protocols and connect to classless provider domains via classless peering to enable uniform deployment of Class A space.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives a simple rule: only give out Class A blocks to networks that have already switched to the new system, or are isolated with no other networks using Class A, or are willing to switch. To make widespread Class A deployment work, everyone needs to switch eventually.

references.text: Fuller, V., T. Li, J. Yu, and K. Varadhan, "Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR): an Address Assignment and Aggregation Strategy", RFC 1519, BARRnet, cisco, MERIT, OARnet, September 1993.
